title: A rejected bow and a shared chariot
intro: Pandarus’ frustration produces a conditional curse against himself. Aeneas redirects him toward a joint attack and offers a choice of roles. The conversation is full of dual pronouns and verbs because both the men and the horses form pairs.

notes.text: πίσυνος means ‘trusting in,’ with dative τόξοισιν. ὀνήσειν is future active infinitive of ὀνίνημι, ‘benefit,’ after ἔμελλον. δοιοῖσιν means ‘two,’ agreeing with ἀριστήεσσιν, epic dative plural of ἀριστεύς. ἔσσευα is aorist of σεύω, ‘set flowing’; ἀτρεκές is adverbial ‘truly, certainly.’

The son of Atreus here is Menelaus, wounded by Pandarus in Book 4, not Agamemnon. ἀμφοτέροιιν is genitive dual after ἐκ. ἤγειρα is aorist of ἐγείρω, ‘roused’; μᾶλλον gives the bitter result: instead of stopping them he only stirred them up further.

αἶσα is an allotted portion or fate; the dative phrase means ‘with an evil destiny / to my misfortune.’ ἑλόμην is second-aorist middle of αἱρέω, ‘took for myself,’ the bow from its peg (πάσσαλος). φέρων χάριν with dative Ἕκτορι means ‘doing Hector a favour.’ The dative ἤματι specifies the day when he took it down.

νοστήσω, ‘return,’ belongs to νοστέω; ἐσόψομαι is future middle of εἰσοράω, ‘see again / behold.’ τάμοι is third-singular second-aorist optative of τέμνω, ‘may [someone] cut off.’ κάρη is an epic accusative ‘head,’ and φώς means ‘man,’ not φῶς, ‘light.’ The optative is a wish forming the sanction of his vow.

θείην is first-singular root-aorist optative of τίθημι: ‘if I do not put this bow in the fire.’ διακλάσσας is aorist participle of διακλάω, ‘break to pieces,’ with epic -σσ-. ἀνεμώλια, ‘windy, useless,’ agrees with τόξα; neuter plural takes singular ὀπηδεῖ, ‘accompanies / serves.’ The bow has become an ineffectual companion.

Aeneas insists that things will not change before they make the attempt. πρίν introduces an infinitive, πειρηθῆναι, aorist passive-form infinitive of πειράω with the sense ‘try / put it to the test.’ νώ is the first-person dual pronoun, and ἐλθόντε its dual participle. ἀντιβίην means ‘face to face, in direct combat’; ἔντεα are fighting gear.

ἐπιβήσεο is a second-singular future middle with imperative force, ‘mount.’ ἴδηαι is epic second-singular aorist middle subjunctive from the ἰδ- stem of seeing: ‘so you may see.’ διωκέμεν is an epic infinitive of διώκω, ‘pursue.’ φέβεσθαι here is ‘flee’; the horses are trained for both pursuit and retreat.

πεδίοιο is a genitive of place over which the horses move, ‘across the plain.’ κραιπνά is adverbial, ‘swiftly.’ τώ refers to the two horses; νῶϊ is their object, ‘us two.’ σαώσετον is third-person dual future of σαόω, ‘will save.’ πόλινδε carries the directional suffix -δε, ‘to the city.’

δέξαι is aorist middle imperative of δέχομαι, ‘take’ whip and reins. δέδεξο is perfect middle imperative of the same verb, ‘stand ready to receive / face’ Diomedes. Aeneas offers either to fight while Pandarus drives or to drive while Pandarus fights. μελήσουσιν … ἐμοί means ‘the horses will be my concern.’

τεώ is the epic possessive ‘your,’ dual agreeing with ἵππω. εἰωθότι is dative perfect participle of ἔθω, ‘accustomed / familiar,’ with ἡνιόχῳ, ‘driver.’ οἴσετον is third-dual future of φέρω, ‘will carry,’ with ἅρμα as object. The horses will respond better to their familiar charioteer.

φεβώμεθα is first-plural middle subjunctive of φέβομαι, ‘flee,’ in an eventual condition. δείσαντε is nominative dual aorist participle of δείδω, ‘be frightened.’ μή introduces Pandarus’ apprehension: the pair may panic and run astray (ματήσετον, dual future of ματάω). The thought continues on the next page.
